analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies where the CEO makes vastly more than the median worker.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 17, 2021 and never received a committee vote or floor action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large corporations whose CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio exceeds 50 to 1 would pay a higher corporate income tax rate: the standard 21% rate would rise by 0.5 percentage points at 50-to-1, climbing in steps to an additional 5 percentage points for companies with pay ratios above 500 to 1. The bill exempts private companies with less than $100 million in average annual gross receipts and directs Treasury to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio by swapping employees for contractors. The idea is to tax companies most for extreme pay gaps and give them a financial reason to narrow them.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large, profitable companies, if employers respond to the higher tax by narrowing the gap between executive pay and median wages. It also modestly raises revenue from the corporations with the widest gaps.

how_it_helps.text: Companies with a pay ratio above 50 to 1 pay a surtax on top of the 21% corporate rate, growing in steps to +5 percentage points for ratios above 500 to 1, so the widest pay gaps cost the most.
The bill authorizes Treasury regulations specifically to prevent companies from manipulating the ratio by using contractors instead of employees, closing an obvious avoidance route.
Companies with average annual gross receipts under $100 million are exempt, so the penalty targets only large corporations.

analysis.who_pays: Large public and private corporations (over $100 million in gross receipts) with extreme executive pay gaps, which would owe a higher tax rate. Some of that cost could ultimately be passed to shareholders or workers through lower investment or pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with big pay gaps

drawbacks.text: A corporate tax increase does not force any company to change its pay structure; firms may simply pay the tax, and economists debate how much of a corporate tax increase is passed on to shareholders, workers, or prices.

The bill creates a compliance burden: companies not currently required to file SEC pay-ratio disclosures (private firms over $100 million in receipts) would have to calculate and report pay ratios under Treasury-prescribed methods.

Because the penalty applies only above 50 to 1, it does nothing for companies with pay ratios of, say, 45 to 1, and the step schedule (0.5 points up to 4 points for ratios between 50 and 500 to 1) gives most affected firms only a small nudge; the 5-point maximum hits only the most extreme ratios.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted, escalating tax penalty aimed at one of the most visible symbols of economic inequality: giant corporations paying top executives hundreds of times what their median worker earns. Its real benefit depends on whether companies change pay practices or just absorb the tax, and the modest penalty sizes for most affected firms (as little as 0.5 points) suggest it works more by signaling and pressure than by force. The costs are borne by the corporations themselves, with some risk of pass-through, and the bill explicitly tries to close the contractor loophole. It is a moderate, workable design rather than a sweeping fix.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill and sent it to the Finance Committee, where it sat without a vote, markup, or floor action for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on March 17, 2021, joined by Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Chris Van Hollen, and Ed Markey as cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
No further action was taken: the Finance Committee never reported the bill, and it never received a floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with the widest CEO-to-worker pay gaps avoided the higher tax rate, since the bill died in committee without a vote. Workers who might have benefited from pressure on executive pay structures saw no change.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big corporations with wide pay gaps

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill proposing corporate tax increases tied to CEO-to-worker pay ratios.

against.name: Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, took no action on the bill after its referral — no markup, no vote, no report — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All four supporters were Sanders plus three Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Democratic-held Senate.

industries.industry: Large corporations with extreme executive pay gaps
industries.note: These firms would owe 0.5 to 5 additional percentage points on their corporate tax, with the largest penalties on the widest gaps, giving them a direct financial incentive to raise median pay or trim executive compensation. The bill explicitly directs Treasury to stop them from dodging the ratio by using contractors.

industries.industry: Private companies with $100M–$1B in gross receipts
industries.note: Firms over the $100 million threshold that are not SEC-registered would face new pay-ratio calculation and reporting requirements and potentially the tax itself; smaller private firms are exempt entirely.
